newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale prices retreat again in February.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale prices retreat again in February.

text.p: Prices at the wholesale level dropped for the second month in a row in February, the government said on Friday, even as the nearly six-year-old economic expansion showed little evidence of fatigue.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.4 percent after declining 0.3 percent in January as both food and energy costs gave ground.

At the same time, the Federal Reserve reported that industrial production rose 0.5 percent in February, while the Commerce Department said business inventories remained lean, auguring well for humming factories in coming months.

The new data adds fuel to the debate on whether the Fed, when its policy-makers meet on March 25, will decide to notch interest rates a little higher for the first time in nearly two years to keep a lid on inflation.

The Fed, which last raised rates on Feb 1,1995, has not changed them since Jan. 31, 1996, when it cut the Federal Funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for short-term loans, to 5.25 percent from 5.5 percent, and the discount rate it charges banks for loans to 5.0 percent from 5.25 percent.
"This is one day that encapsulates the Fed's dilemma," said First Chicago NBD chief economist James Annable. "This is strong growth in the economy and yet we don't have much sign of inflation."

CIBC Wood Gundy Securities chief economist Joseph Liro, commenting on the Producer Price Index, took the view that the Fed will "need at least one bad inflation number before they can pull the trigger (on higher interest rates), and there's nothing in this number that you can point to."

The so-called core rate, which excludes the often-volatile food and energy sector and which economists believe more closely tracks inflation, also declined, falling 0.1 percent in February after being unchanged in January.
The report was far better than Wall Street predictions, which saw overall wholesale prices falling 0.1 percent and the core rate edging up 0.1 percent.

The department said energy prices fell 1.2 percent in February after a decline of 0.2 percent in January. Gasoline prices retreated 3.1 percent after jumping 2.6 percent, while home heating oil was off 1.1 percent after falling 2.8 percent in January.
Food prices also fell, dropping 0.3 percent after moving 1.0 percent lower in January, as meat and fish costs turned down.
The department also noted that computer prices in February fell a record 5.2 percent, eclipsing the previous record fall of 4.0 percent in July 1991.
Auto prices, which fell 0.4 percent in January, rose 0.2 percent in Feburary, the department said.
Goods at the intermediate level of production, which require additional processing, fell 0.1 percent after being up 0.2 percent in January.
Prices at the early part of the production cycle, so-called crude goods, fell 5.9 percent in February after rising 5.2 percent in the prior month.

In its report, the Fed said strong manufacturing activity boosted the nation's industrial output during February. But the report showed no sign of developing production bottlenecks, sometimes a signal of oncoming inflation pressures.
Industrial production climbed 0.5 percent after a revised 0.1 percent drop in January, the strongest monthly pickup in output since a 0.8 percent jump last November.

Yet the capacity use rate -- a potential measure of inflation pressures -- barely edged up, to 83.3 percent from a revised 83.2 percent in January and remained below the 83.5 percent operating rate reached last December.
Inventories held by businesses edged up only slightly in January as more goods remained on the shelves of manufacturers and wholesalers.
Total inventories rose 0.1 percent in January to a seasonally adjusted $1.01 trillion after dropping 0.1 percent in December.
The inventory-to-sales ratio -- a gauge of how long it would take to sell existing stocks at the current pace -- fell to 1.37 months' worth in January from 1.39 in December.
